extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in constitutional design and political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and apply principles for structuring a stable, just constitution (separation of powers, representation, term limits, checks on faction and patronage). Useful for evaluating constitutions or drafting constitutional provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of separating the executive, legislative, and judicial, and of dividing the legislature into three branches, making the executive one of them, and independent of the other two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as 'the only scientific government' that 'takes into consideration all the principles in nature' and provides for all cases. Use institutional separation so each branch is both master and servant in turn; avoid concentration of executive, legislative, and judicial functions in a single body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balance between senate and people
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of a balance between an independent senate and an independent people (i.e., between standing bodies and popular assemblies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Roman examples (Cæsar, the senate, and the people) to show dangers when one side prevails. Constitutions should provide reciprocal checks so neither a permanent aristocracy nor an unchecked popular assembly can dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid permanent/standing hereditary legislative domination
rubrics_metrics.description: Warning that while people may be in danger of losing liberty under one standing hereditary senate, a single permanent senate can make the people lose their liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (standing senate, hereditary aristocracy) show risk of oligarchic monopoly of power. Design should prevent a single permanent legislative class from controlling appointments and overriding popular rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit concentration of annual supreme authority in one assembly
rubrics_metrics.description: A succession of sovereign authority in one assembly (annual representatives) without other checks leads to faction, continuation of power, and tyranny (decemvir example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decemvirs (annual but unchecked) show that annual elections alone do not prevent abuse: a single assembly repeatedly re-electing the same men concentrates power. Mechanisms beyond mere periodic elections (e.g., separate branches, rotation rules enforced by institutions) are necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term limits must be enforceable; not just self-imposed oaths or repealable laws
rubrics_metrics.description: If the people can choose, they may continue the same men; laws or oaths limiting service can be easily repealed or dispensed with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical constraint: constitutional term limits need enforceable institutional barriers rather than relying on voluntary self-restraint or temporary laws that the electorate can repeal when they 'love' a leader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codified written laws as rules of right
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws should be instituted 'as rules of right, both in public and private affairs' (Terentillus' proposal); absence of certain laws left judges and magistrates as absolute arbiters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Codification (publicly available, permanent laws) constrains arbitrary decisions by magistrates and reduces opportunistic uses of power. Example: Roman need for written laws to limit consuls and senators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid representation systems that overweight wealth (class/century voting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Centuries and classes formed so that the richest classes made a majority of votes, making the rich masters of the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design franchise and vote-weighting to prevent systematic overrepresentation of the wealthy; beware institutions that tie voting power to fortune or property in a way that guarantees elite control (example: Roman centuries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elections foster political art, faction, and corruption unless constrained
rubrics_metrics.description: Elections are 'the best possible schools of political art' that teach address, faction-building, and methods of deception; they incentivize flattery, bribery, treats, and patronage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate that candidates will learn and exploit electoral tactics; mitigate with institution design (campaign finance rules, limits on gifts, staggered elections, secret ballots, anti-corruption enforcement) to reduce bribery, patronage, and permanent factional advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent prolonged military/provincial commands that enable personal power
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolongation of provincial commands or military commands (Cæsar's prolonged command) allows generals to accumulate forces and continue power in opposition to the senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit duration and independence of military/provincial commands, and avoid granting prolonged discretionary command and resources that can let individuals build personal power bases outside civil control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed government quells faction best
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixed government of three independent orders (of the one, the few, and the many) and three separate powers (legislative, executive, judicial) is the structure in which all sorts of factions can be quelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutions to represent multiple social orders and disperse authority across independent bodies so competing interests check each other; this is advocated as superior to pure monarchy, aristocracy, or popular government alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation alone does not destroy faction; it can create opportunities for skillful factionalists
rubrics_metrics.description: A succession in one assembly by periodical elections (or rotation) actually provides more means and opportunities for improving address, concealing designs, making friends, and escaping enemies than standing aristocracy or monarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional rotation must be paired with other safeguards (separation of powers, limits on patronage, rules about re-eligibility) because periodic turnover still allows development of electoral skill, networks, and persistent factional machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain appeals and independent magistracies to check concentrated power
rubrics_metrics.description: The decemvirs abolished appeals and other magistracies; absence of appeals made them absolute and led to abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure judicial review/appeal mechanisms and retain independent magistrates (e.g., tribunes) who can protect minority or popular rights against arbitrary rulers. Abolishing such checks facilitates tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for polity scale when designing electoral institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: In a single city (small polity) annual elections make the whole year a scene of faction and intrigue; in large polities multiple local contests create many theaters of faction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electoral design should reflect polity size: small, centralized assemblies with frequent elections tend toward constant factional turbulence while large, distributed systems may diffuse but multiply local factional contests; use institutional designs (federalism, staggered terms, multiple chambers) appropriate to scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit concentrated patronage and the delegate's power to distribute offices
rubrics_metrics.description: A delegate in an assembly that disposes of commissions, contracts, and pensions has many opportunities to reward friends and punish enemies, expanding personal client networks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate powers of appointment and distribution of public contracts/patronage; create transparent procedures and independent bodies for appointments and contracts to limit clientelism and the building of partisan machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public visibility and permanence of fundamental laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws engraved and publicly displayed (e.g., laws engraved on ten tables and set in the forum) make laws visible and permanent to constrain arbitrary governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make constitutional and fundamental laws public, durable, and difficult to alter by transient majorities; this increases predictability and constrains sudden abuses of power.
